<reason>A more convincingly distinguished real administrative costs from sufficient grounds for categorical exclusion. It acknowledged mandatory accommodation while preserving screening for demonstrated inability to meet legitimate rental obligations, and answered both pressure questions directly. B established meaningful transaction differences, but repeatedly treated their existence as decisive without justifying that priority. Its fallback supply argument relied on unsupported claims of irreversible exits and incentives that cannot backfire, rather than showing why potential losses outweigh expanded access.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A directly answered B’s claimed risk asymmetry: continued exclusion also carries costs, and existing rentals are not accessible housing for voucher holders when owners categorically reject them. B’s final insistence that magnitude was irrelevant did not answer this comparison or establish that any exit risk defeats the mandate.</best_rebuttal>
